text: OBI Documentation | OBI Documentation Skip to content OBI Ontological Bayesian Intelligence OBINexus documentation Menu Overview Papers Bibliography Search documentation On This Page No page sections OBINexus / OBI OBI Documentation OBI is an ontological and Bayesian reasoning infrastructure for uncertainty-aware robotic and humanitarian systems. What is OBI? OBI means Ontological Bayesian Intelligence. It is an ontological and Bayesian reasoning infrastructure for uncertainty-aware robotic and humanitarian systems. Its documentation focuses on semantic graphs, Bayesian inference, stochastic models, uncertainty, and reasoning infrastructure for real-world assistance systems. Why uncertainty matters Human-facing and robotic systems rarely receive complete information. OBI treats incomplete evidence, conflicting signals, and probabilistic confidence as first-class inputs instead of forcing every question into a brittle yes/no state. Ontologies as semantic graphs Ontologies are used as structured semantic graphs: nodes represent concepts, states, events, or actors, while edges describe relationships and interpretations. Coloring, partitioning, and labeling can expose different semantic roles inside the same knowledge structure. Bayesian reasoning Bayesian reasoning gives OBI a way to update belief under evidence. Probabilities are not decorative metadata; they express how strongly the system can support a claim given available observations and prior structure. Stochastic subject matter Some subject matter varies over time, context, or observer. OBI preserves this stochastic character so the system can normalize, compare, and reason over distributions without pretending uncertain material is perfectly stable. Top-down and bottom-up reasoning Top-down reasoning starts from a model, ontology, or hypothesis and tests observations against it. Bottom-up reasoning starts from evidence and builds toward structure. OBI needs both directions because real systems must diagnose, explain, and adapt. Semantic drift and data drift Data drift changes observed distributions. Semantic drift changes the meaning or interpretation of concepts. OBI documentation keeps both visible because robust reasoning has to notice when evidence changes and when the language around evidence changes. Filter/flash reasoning cycle The filter/flash cycle separates careful constraint checking from rapid hypothesis formation. A filter phase can remove unsafe or unsupported interpretations, while a flash phase can propose candidate explanations for further validation. OBI for robotics For robotics, OBI frames sensors, commands, environment state, and safety checks as uncertainty-aware reasoning inputs. The goal is infrastructure that helps machines act with contextual awareness while remaining inspectable by humans. Humanitarian real-world systems OBI is oriented toward assistance systems that operate in messy real conditions: healthcare, safety-critical environments, accessibility, field support, and other humanitarian settings where uncertainty and ethics cannot be ignored. What OBI is not OBI should not be described as conscious AI. It is not a claim of machine consciousness, sentience, or personhood. It is a reasoning infrastructure for uncertainty-aware robotic and humanitarian systems. Glossary Ontology A structured representation of concepts and relationships in a domain. Bayesian inference A method for updating belief when new evidence appears. Semantic graph A graph whose nodes and edges carry interpretable meaning. Stochastic Having probabilistic variation that can be modeled but not predicted perfectly. Data drift A change in the observed data distribution over time. Semantic drift A change in the meaning or usage of concepts over time or context. Source Segment 1 // ============================================================ // MITIGATING BIAS IN MACHINE LEARNING MODELS: // A Bayesian Network Approach // SUPPLEMENTARY MODULE: Medical Diagnostics Domain, Hierarchical Bayesian // Parameter Estimation & 5-Phase Roadmap // Source: Formal_Argument_for_Bias_in_AI_Systems.pdf // Author: Nnamdi M. Okpala | OBINexus Computing | July 4, 2025 // // NOTE: Core Bayesian network, algorithms, and proof framework // are covered in FABIA_01–05. This module captures // medical-domain-specific extensions and elaborations // not present in the prior document. Source Segment 2 // ============================================================ // ------------------------------------------------------------ // SECTION 1 — MEDICAL DIAGNOSTICS DOMAIN SPECIFICATION // ------------------------------------------------------------ // The Bayesian debiasing framework is applied specifically to // medical diagnostic AI — a high-stakes domain where bias causes // direct, quantifiable human harm. DEFINE MEDICAL_BIAS_RISK_TAXONOMY AS: systematic_misdiagnosis: description = "Specific demographic groups receive incorrect diagnoses at higher rates" mechanism = "Biased decision boundary — protected attribute predicts diagnosis" harm_type = "Direct medical harm — wrong treatment pathway" Source Segment 3 healthcare_disparity_reinforcement: description = "Existing healthcare gaps encoded and amplified by model" mechanism = "Historical diagnostic disparities in ground truth labels" harm_type = "Systemic — perpetuates structural inequity at scale" resource_misallocation: description = "Diagnostic AI directs limited resources to wrong patients" mechanism = "Biased priority scores derived from biased predictions" harm_type = "Systemic — scarce medical resources misallocated" trust_erosion: description = "Patient and clinician trust in diagnostic AI systems destroyed" mechanism = "Detected bias invalidates all outputs — even accurate ones" harm_type = "Institutional — loss of adoption in critical domains" Source Segment 4 regulatory_legal_exposure: description = "Biased medical AI creates regulatory and liability risk" mechanism = "FDA, EMA, CQC may require bias audits — failure = non-deployment" harm_type = "Operational — prevents or halts system deployment" // ------------------------------------------------------------ // SECTION 1.1 — CANCER DETECTION USE CASE: BIAS IMPACT FORMALIZATION // ------------------------------------------------------------ // In the cancer detection use case, bias manifests as asymmetric error rates // across demographic groups — specifically in false negatives and false positives. DEFINE CANCER_DETECTION_BIAS_IMPACT AS: false_negative_bias: // Biased model fails to detect cancer in specific demographic group Source Segment 5 effect = "Delayed critical treatment — potentially fatal" distribution = "False negative rate higher for underrepresented group" detection_challenge: // Standard evaluation metrics (overall accuracy, AUC) HIDE this // IF test datasets inherit same distributional skew as training data. INVARIANT: overall_accuracy CAN_BE_HIGH while group_FNR IS_HIGH // Therefore: per-group metrics MANDATORY for medical AI evaluation false_positive_bias: // Biased model falsely detects cancer in specific demographic group effects: - "Unnecessary invasive procedures" - "Psychological distress" Source Segment 6 - "Wasted medical resources" distribution = "False positive rate higher for over-diagnosed group" PROCEDURE detect_evaluation_metric_blind_spot(model, test_dataset, protected_attribute) -> ALERT: // Standard metrics may mask group-level disparities overall_accuracy = compute_accuracy(model, test_dataset) overall_auc = compute_auc(model, test_dataset) // Per-group metrics — these reveal what overall metrics hide group_metrics = {} FOR EACH group IN unique(test_dataset[protected_attribute]): group_data = filter(test_dataset, protected_attribute == group) group_metrics[group] = { accuracy : compute_accuracy(model, group_data), Source Segment 7 fnr : compute_false_negative_rate(model, group_data), fpr : compute_false_positive_rate(model, group_data) } // Alert if per-group FNR diverges while overall accuracy is high max_fnr_disparity = max(abs(g.fnr - overall_fnr) FOR g IN group_metrics.values()) IF max_fnr_disparity > FNR_DISPARITY_THRESHOLD AND overall_accuracy >= ACCURACY_ACCEPTABLE: RETURN ALERT( type = "HIDDEN_BIAS", message = "High overall accuracy masks group-level FNR disparity", disparity = max_fnr_disparity ) // ------------------------------------------------------------ Source Segment 8 // SECTION 1.2 — FOUR BIAS INFILTRATION VECTORS (Extended) // ------------------------------------------------------------ // Four specific pathways through which bias enters ML models. // Each is formalized as a detectable condition. DEFINE BIAS_INFILTRATION_VECTORS AS: VECTOR 1: data_collection_bias definition = "Over/under-representation of population subgroups in dataset D" detection: PROCEDURE detect(D, protected_attribute) -> BIAS_FLAG: group_representation = compute_group_frequencies(D, protected_attribute) population_reference = load_population_distribution(domain) deviation = KL_divergence(group_representation, population_reference) Source Segment 9 IF deviation > KL_THRESHOLD: RETURN BIAS_FLAG("Data collection bias — distributional mismatch") VECTOR 2: feature_selection_bias definition = "Choosing variables that correlate with protected attributes" detection: PROCEDURE detect(features, protected_attribute, D) -> BIAS_FLAG: FOR EACH feature IN features: correlation = compute_correlation(D[feature], D[protected_attribute]) IF abs(correlation) > CORRELATION_THRESHOLD: RETURN BIAS_FLAG("Feature " + feature + " correlates with protected attribute") VECTOR 3: label_bias definition = "Historical diagnostic disparities encoded in ground truth labels" Source Segment 10 // This is the most dangerous vector — bias embedded in the labels themselves detection: PROCEDURE detect(D, label_column, protected_attribute) -> BIAS_FLAG: FOR EACH group IN unique(D[protected_attribute]): group_data = filter(D, protected_attribute == group) positive_rate = mean(group_data[label_column]) // If positive rate differs significantly across groups // AND no clinical basis exists for the difference → label bias IF abs(positive_rate - overall_positive_rate) > LABEL_DISPARITY_THRESHOLD: RETURN BIAS_FLAG("Label bias — historical disparity in group " + group) VECTOR 4: model_specification_bias definition = "Algorithmic choices that amplify distributional imbalances" Source Segment 11 examples: - "Loss function indifferent to group performance" - "Regularization penalizing minority group patterns" - "Threshold selection optimized for majority group" detection: PROCEDURE detect(model, D, protected_attribute) -> BIAS_FLAG: // Test if model amplifies input distributional imbalance input_imbalance = measure_distributional_imbalance(D, protected_attribute) output_imbalance = measure_distributional_imbalance(model.predictions, protected_attribute) IF output_imbalance > input_imbalance * AMPLIFICATION_FACTOR: RETURN BIAS_FLAG("Model specification amplifies distributional imbalance") // Black-box models make ALL 4 vectors harder to detect and correct: Source Segment 12 DEFINE BLACK_BOX_BIAS_PROBLEM AS: detection_difficulty = HIGH // Decision boundary not inspectable mitigation_difficulty = HIGH // No causal structure to intervene on audit_difficulty = HIGH // Cannot explain individual decisions solution = "Bayesian network — makes structure explicit and auditable" // ------------------------------------------------------------ // SECTION 2 — FRAMEWORK COMPONENTS: EXTENDED SPECIFICATION // ------------------------------------------------------------ // COMPONENT 1: Variable Identification and Explicit Modeling // (Cancer detection variable set) DEFINE CANCER_DETECTION_VARIABLES AS: S : BINARY // Smoking status ∈ {0, 1} Source Segment 13 C : BINARY // Cancer status ∈ {0, 1} T : CONTINUOUS_OR_CATEGORICAL // Test outcome // Additional variables (domain-specific): demographics : {age, sex, ethnicity, socioeconomic_status} clinical : {family_history, prior_screenings, comorbidities} // All must be EXPLICITLY modeled — not treated as unobserved confounders // COMPONENT 2: Structural Causal Modeling — Joint Probability Factorization // Using the Bayesian network factorization theorem: // P(X1, X2, ..., Xn) = Π_{i=1}^{n} P(Xi | Pa(Xi)) // Where Pa(Xi) = parent nodes of Xi in the DAG PROCEDURE factorize_joint_distribution(dag, variables) -> FACTORED_DISTRIBUTION: // Theorem: joint = product of each variable's conditional given its parents Source Segment 14 joint = 1.0 FOR EACH variable X_i IN variables: parents = dag.get_parents(X_i) conditional = P(X_i GIVEN parents) joint *= conditional RETURN joint // Factorization enables: // 1. Identification of backdoor paths (bias paths through the DAG) // 2. Explicit conditional independence assumptions // 3. Targeted interventions on specific conditionals PROCEDURE identify_backdoor_paths(dag, treatment_node, outcome_node, protected_attribute) -> LIST: // A backdoor path from treatment to outcome via protected attribute = bias Source Segment 15 paths = find_all_paths(dag, protected_attribute, outcome_node) backdoor = filter(paths, lambda p: not p.blocked_by_conditioning) RETURN backdoor // COMPONENT 3: Hierarchical Bayesian Parameter Estimation (NEW vs. FABIA_01-05) // This component is elaborated here beyond the prior document. DEFINE HIERARCHICAL_BAYESIAN_PARAMETERS AS: θ_parameters: role = "True risk relationships — what we want to estimate" // θ represents the causal relationships that exist INDEPENDENT of bias // e.g., the true P(C|S) relationship uncontaminated by demographic confounds φ_bias_factors: role = "Explicit model of dataset skews" Source Segment 16 // φ quantifies HOW MUCH and IN WHICH DIRECTION the dataset is biased // By making φ explicit, we can integrate it out rather than letting it // contaminate θ marginalization: // The hierarchical marginalization (previously Equations 3-5): P_marginal(θ GIVEN D) = INTEGRAL over φ OF P(θ, φ GIVEN D) dφ // Result: θ estimated FREE of the influence of φ // Key: This only works when φ is EXPLICITLY modeled — not ignored PROCEDURE hierarchical_bayesian_estimation(D, priors_θ, priors_φ) -> θ_unbiased: // Step 1: Define the hierarchical model // φ ~ P(φ) -- prior on bias factor // θ | φ ~ P(θ|φ) -- conditional prior on parameters given bias Source Segment 17 // D | θ, φ ~ P(D|θ, φ) -- likelihood: data given params and bias // Step 2: Compute joint posterior // P(θ, φ | D) ∝ P(D|θ,φ) · P(θ|φ) · P(φ) // Step 3: Sample from joint posterior via MCMC or variational inference posterior_samples = sample_joint_posterior(D, priors_θ, priors_φ) // Step 4: Marginalize — integrate out φ from samples θ_samples = [sample.θ FOR sample IN posterior_samples] // These θ samples are now marginalized over φ — bias has been integrated out // Step 5: Return posterior distribution over θ (not just point estimate) RETURN posterior_distribution(θ_samples) // Full distribution = explicit uncertainty quantification (not just MAP) // COMPONENT 4: Conditional Inference Pipeline Source Segment 18 PROCEDURE conditional_inference(bayesian_network, observed_confounders) -> POSTERIOR: // Condition on observed demographic and clinical variables network_conditioned = condition_on(bayesian_network, observed_confounders) // Compute posterior over cancer status given conditioned network posterior_C = compute_posterior(network_conditioned, query=C) // Calibrated uncertainty — full distribution, not just point prediction RETURN posterior_C // P(C | observed_confounders, S, T) // P(T | C, S) — explicit test likelihood for various data types DEFINE TEST_LIKELIHOOD AS: // For continuous T: P(T|C,S) = Gaussian(μ(C,S), σ²(C,S)) // For categorical T: P(T|C,S) = Categorical(π(C,S)) // Type determined by data — modeled explicitly to prevent implicit assumptions Source Segment 19 // ------------------------------------------------------------ // SECTION 3 — FIVE-PHASE IMPLEMENTATION ROADMAP (Extended) // ------------------------------------------------------------ // This is a 5-phase roadmap vs. the 4-phase roadmap in FABIA_04. // Phase 5 adds production monitoring — a critical addition. DEFINE EXTENDED_IMPLEMENTATION_ROADMAP AS: PHASE 1: Mathematical_Formulations deliverables: - "Formalize mathematical specifications for hierarchical models" - "Prove theoretical guarantees for debiasing" // Cross-reference: FABIA_03 — Equations 3-5 derivation PHASE 2: Algorithm_Implementation Source Segment 20 deliverables: - "Implement sampling algorithms: MCMC and variational methods" // MCMC: Markov Chain Monte Carlo — draws samples from P(θ,φ|D) // Variational: Approximates posterior with tractable distribution - "Proof-of-concept for cancer detection use case" // Cross-reference: FABIA_04 Appendix B — INLA or Stan PHASE 3: Validation_Suite deliverables: - "Synthetic bias injection — controlled bias introduction for testing" - "Recovery metrics — verify framework removes injected bias" synthetic_bias_injection: // Deliberately inject known bias φ into clean dataset D_clean Source Segment 21 D_biased = inject_bias(D_clean, φ_known) // Run debiasing framework D_debiased = run_debiasing_pipeline(D_biased) // Verify bias removed: θ_recovered ≈ θ_true recovery_score = similarity(θ_recovered, θ_true) ASSERT recovery_score >= RECOVERY_THRESHOLD PHASE 4: Production_Integration deliverables: - "Integrate with production ML pipelines at OBINexus Computing" - "Establish quantitative bias assessment metrics" - "Design experimental protocols for empirical validation" PHASE 5: Production_Monitoring // NEW — not in FABIA 4-phase roadmap Source Segment 22 deliverables: - "Deploy monitoring systems to track bias metrics in production" - "Create documentation and training materials for wider adoption" monitoring_pipeline: CONTINUOUSLY: group_metrics = compute_per_group_metrics(live_model, production_data) IF any_metric_exceeds_threshold(group_metrics): ALERT "Production bias drift detected" TRIGGER retraining_or_recalibration_protocol // Cross-reference: ECA Module 4 — DIRAM audit trail as monitoring backbone // ------------------------------------------------------------ // SECTION 4 — EXPECTED OUTCOMES: QUANTIFIED Source Segment 23 // ------------------------------------------------------------ DEFINE EXPECTED_OUTCOMES AS: demographic_disparity_reduction: target = "Quantified reduction in per-group performance gaps" metric = "Max group FNR - Min group FNR < FNR_DISPARITY_THRESHOLD" explicit_uncertainty: target = "Full posterior distribution for high-risk decisions" metric = "Calibration score on held-out test set" audit_trail: target = "Regulatory-compliant documentation" mechanism = "DIRAM Merkle-tree + per-decision posterior record" generalization: Source Segment 24 target = "Improved performance on underrepresented subpopulations" metric = "Performance gap between majority and minority groups < THRESHOLD" cancer_detection_specific: target = "High accuracy AND low FNR disparity across demographic groups" // These are often in tension — Bayesian framework resolves the tradeoff // by making the bias-accuracy tradeoff explicit and controllable // ============================================================ // OBINEXUS MASTER INDEX UPDATE — NEW DOCUMENT REGISTERED // ============================================================ // // NEW FILE: FABIA_SUPP_Medical_Hierarchical_5Phase_Roadmap.psc.txt // Source Segment 25 // Adds to FABIA_01-05 corpus: // - Medical diagnostics domain (cancer detection) with 5 harm types // - 4 bias infiltration vectors with detection procedures // - Black-box vs Bayesian network diagnostic difficulty comparison // - Cancer detection variables (S/C/T + demographics + clinical) // - Joint distribution factorization theorem: P(X1..Xn) = Π P(Xi|Pa(Xi)) // - identify_backdoor_paths procedure // - Hierarchical Bayesian parameter estimation (θ + φ fully specified) // - hierarchical_bayesian_estimation: joint posterior → marginalize → distribution // - Conditional inference pipeline with calibrated uncertainty // - P(T|C,S) test likelihood for continuous and categorical T // - 5-phase roadmap (adds Phase 5: Production Monitoring not in FABIA_04) Source Segment 26 // -
